result:
Part of the premise is true. Labs do use reinforcement learning (RL) to train the models that agents run on. But for your makerspace assistant, training your own model isn't the right move. Your `MISSION.md` also lists training and the math inside models as out of scope, so I'll give you the short version and then point you at what will help more.

**PPO in one worked picture.** Say the model is asked "Is the laser cutter free Friday at 2?" and it picks an action: call `check_calendar`. We score the whole attempt, for example +1 if the booking was right and −1 if not. The simplest RL update raises the probability of actions in good attempts and lowers it in bad ones. That is the policy gradient. It has a flaw: one big update can wreck the model. PPO (Schulman et al., 2017) fixes this in three steps:

1. Measure how much more likely the new model makes an action: r = π_new(action) / π_old(action).
2. Multiply r by the advantage A, which is how much better than average that action turned out.
3. Clip r to the range 1−ε to 1+ε, usually ε ≈ 0.2. The objective is min(r·A, clip(r, 1−ε, 1+ε)·A), so no single update can move the model far.

I've left out the full derivation: the importance-sampling step, the trust-region argument and how A is estimated. You'd need policy-gradient basics before it makes sense, and you don't have those yet.

**Why not train for the makerspace.** Training needs a model you can update, thousands of scored runs, and GPUs. Your budget is small and the design review is in five weeks. You can get most of the tool-calling gain more cheaply:
- Write sharp tool descriptions.
- Write a test set of 30 real student questions with the expected tool calls.
- Iterate on those until the failures stop.

That also covers your goals of writing clear tool descriptions and defending the architecture.

If you do want RL in scope, tell me and I'll update your mission and teach the policy-gradient basics first.

Quick check: in your assistant, what would count as the "score" for a good tool call?
